WEDE5020 / Practice portfolio

Build and publish a repair café website

A campus repair café needs a website where visitors can find the next session, find the venue and check which items volunteers can repair. Use fictional contact and enquiry details.

This 100-mark practice rubric is for self-assessment or peer feedback. Follow your lecturer’s brief and rubric for formal submissions.

Part 1. Plan and structure Part 2. Style and test Final part. Add behaviour and publish Practice rubric

Part 1. Plan and structure

  1. Write a brief naming the target audience, the main visitor task and one measure of success.
  2. Sketch a sitemap and a phone-width homepage wireframe. Record the source and licence for any assets you use.
  3. Build Home, Visit and Enquiries with unique page titles, clear headings and navigation. Give informative images alternative text and label each form field.
  4. Put the work in a GitHub repository. Make separate commits for the structure and content, then test every link from every page.

Submit your brief, sitemap, wireframe, asset credits and repository URL.

Review HTML . Review the GitHub chapter

Part 2. Style and test

  1. Link one external stylesheet across all three pages. Use consistent spacing, colours and typography.
  2. Start with a single-column layout. Use a breakpoint and Flexbox or Grid to arrange session cards when more room is available.
  3. Test at 320px, 768px and desktop width. Tab through links and fields. Check focus indicators and general readability.
  4. Record one layout defect and its fix. Retest it after changing the CSS.

Submit phone and desktop screenshots plus a test log with expected results, actual results, fixes and retest outcomes.

Review CSS . Review responsive design

Final part. Add behaviour and publish

  1. Add a JavaScript filter for supported repair items or a form preview that displays a confirmation using fictional inputs.
  2. Test two normal inputs and one edge case, such as a filter with no matching items. Record what the page displays.
  3. Put the feature on a branch. Open a pull request, describe your tests, inspect the diff and merge it into the publishing branch.
  4. Publish with GitHub Pages. Check every page from the public address, including links from nested pages. Add a README with setup and test instructions.

Submit the repository, merged pull request and live site URLs, your test evidence and a short reflection naming one thing to improve.

Review JavaScript . Review GitHub Pages publishing

Practice rubric

Apply each criterion separately. Award full marks when the listed evidence meets the criterion, partial marks when some evidence is present or has defects, and zero when evidence is missing.

Practice marks out of 100
CriterionEvidence for full marksMarks
PlanningClear audience, goal, sitemap, wireframe and asset credits.10
HTMLThree semantic pages, working navigation, useful alternative text and labelled fields.15
Version controlMeaningful commits documenting the first stage.5
CSSShared stylesheet with coherent typography, spacing and layout.15
Responsive and keyboard useUsable at all three widths, with visible focus and no unintended sideways scrolling.15
Testing and iterationScreenshots and a test log with a recorded fix and retest.5
JavaScriptA working feature with sensible feedback and evidence for normal and edge cases.15
Pull requestA merged feature branch with a clear description and test notes.8
DeploymentPublic Pages site with working navigation, stylesheet and scripts.8
HandoverREADME, working submission links and a specific improvement for a future version.4
TotalPart 1: 30. Part 2: 35. Final part: 35.100

Before you submit

  • Open the repository, pull request and site URLs in a private browsing window.
  • Check every link and control with a keyboard and at phone width.
  • Confirm the live version matches the merged work and uses only fictional data.
  • Use the rubric to identify one weak criterion and fix it before submission.
